title: Knowledge Check 6 - Lessons 26-30
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-30 - Access to Records | Access to Other Data. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: An external partner must see records owned by their internal account manager but nothing else sensitive. What is the cleanest configuration?
options: Give the partner an external role under the account manager's role plus relationship-based sharing sets, and keep OWD restrictive
Relax OWD to Public Read Only
Make the partner a system admin
questions.explanation: An external role under the manager gives hierarchy access to the manager's owned records, while sharing sets handle relationship access and OWD stays restrictive - least privilege without over-exposure.

questions.question: Which control is essential to protect sensitive fields from external portal users even when record access is correctly limited?
options: Field-level security and masking on the portal profile
questions.explanation: FLS and masking hide sensitive fields from the portal profile regardless of record access. Roles, public OWD, and View All all broaden rather than protect exposure.

questions.question: What is the primary data-protection risk of giving external users a high role in the role hierarchy?
options: They gain hierarchy access to records owned below that role, potentially including unrelated internal data
questions.explanation: A high role grants upward-hierarchy access to records owned below it, which can expose unrelated internal data. Place external roles as low as needed.

questions.question: An org wants to share records by a business process that maps to a Record Type. Which pattern best drives access?
options: Stamp the record type and create a criteria-based sharing rule referencing it
questions.explanation: Driving a criteria-based sharing rule off the stamped record type gives process-based access declaratively. View All, teams, and public OWD over-grant or are record-specific.

questions.question: What is the key trade-off between a stored stamp field and a formula/rollup for driving sharing?
options: Stamps are stored and must be kept in sync but query fast; formulas/rollups compute automatically but add compute cost
Only rollups can be used in sharing
questions.explanation: Stored stamps are fast and stable but need sync on change; computed formulas/rollups stay correct automatically but cost compute and have aggregation limits - choose by volume and maintenance needs.

questions.question: Why might a criteria-based rule not share records that were just stamped with the matching value?
options: The rule needs recalculation and the stamp/rule evaluation is asynchronous
questions.explanation: Criteria rule evaluation and recalculation are asynchronous; after stamp values change, the rule's grants can be stale until recalc processes - the expected behavior to plan for.

questions.question: An account owner occasionally needs to let a specific colleague see one record, a one-off human decision. Which mechanism is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Rare, owner-initiated single-record grants are exactly manual sharing. Rules/Apex are for repeatable/computed access, and OWD changes affect everyone.

questions.question: A requirement is repeatable - 'any record whose Type is VIP is visible to the VIP group'. Which override is best?
options: A stamp of the Type value plus a criteria-based sharing rule to the VIP group
questions.explanation: A criteria-based rule driven by the Type stamp expresses the repeatable rule declaratively. Manual shares and Apex per-record do not scale, and teams are per-record ad-hoc.

questions.question: Which situation warrants custom (Apex) sharing logic over stamping?
options: Access derived from an external system's runtime computation that a field cannot represent
questions.explanation: When the access-determining data is computed externally and cannot be stamped, Apex Managed Sharing is required. Simple picklist, one-off, and hierarchy cases are declarative.

questions.question: A manager creates a report in a public folder; each rep who runs it should see only their own team's data. What preserves this?
options: Leave the report run-as the logged-in user
Set the report to run as the manager
Grant View All to all reps
Move the report to a private folder only
questions.explanation: Reports default to run-as the viewing user, so each rep's results reflect their own sharing - exactly the desired behavior. Running as the manager or granting View All would expose all data to everyone.

questions.question: A dashboard summarizes metrics and must NOT reveal other managers' data to a viewer. What is the correct running-user setting?
questions.explanation: Running as the logged-in user filters the dashboard to the viewer's own data access. Running as an admin or owner exposes that person's broader view to every viewer.

questions.question: Why does placing a report in a folder a user can open NOT guarantee they can see the report's records?
options: Report results are filtered by the viewer's own sharing/FLS; folder access only controls who can view/edit the report
questions.explanation: Folder access governs access to the report artifact; the DATA shown is filtered by each viewer's record sharing and field security. The two are independent.

questions.question: A user can open an Account record but cannot see a file attached to it. What is the most likely reason?
options: File access is governed separately from record access - the file isn't shared with that user
The Account is a master record
questions.explanation: File sharing is independent of record sharing; a file attached to a record is only visible to users the file is shared with (via sharing settings, libraries, or record sharing when configured). Record access alone does not grant file access.

questions.question: Which mechanism controls which Knowledge articles a user can view?
options: Article visibility (internal/customer) plus data category security plus the View Articles permission
questions.explanation: Knowledge article visibility combines the user's Knowledge permission with internal/customer visibility and data categories. It is not record-owner or OWD driven.

questions.question: Which statement about custom metadata types is TRUE?
options: They are governed by record sharing rules
They are typically configuration visible to users granted the relevant object permission, protected by the Protected flag in managed packages, and do not follow OWD/sharing
They are always public to all users
questions.explanation: Custom metadata is configuration metadata, not record data; its access is via object permissions and the Protected flag, not the OWD/sharing model.
